title: Tidal Won't Pay Royalties on Fully AI-Made Songs
hook: Tidal isn't banning AI music — but starting July 15, any track it identifies as 100% AI-generated stops earning royalties and gets tagged so listeners know what they're hearing.
key_points: Tidal will label any track it identifies as fully AI-generated with an on-platform tag.
Those tracks lose royalty payments and can't be sold directly to fans, effective July 15, 2026.
Tidal isn't banning AI music outright — only cutting monetization for 100%-AI tracks.
It will also use automated tools to remove AI tracks built to impersonate real artists.
The policy also covers Tidal Upload, the platform's independent-artist program.
content_html: Streaming platforms have mostly danced around AI music instead of setting hard rules. Tidal just picked a side. The Verge reports that starting July 15, 2026, Tidal will label any track it identifies as 100% AI-generated with an on-platform tag — and cut off its royalties and direct-to-fan sales entirely.
extra_html: The key word is fully: Tidal isn't banning AI-assisted music, only music it judges to have no meaningful human creation behind it. Once flagged, a track keeps its place in the catalog but stops making money for whoever uploaded it, and listeners see a badge marking it as AI-made. Tidal is also deploying automated tools to catch and remove a nastier category — AI tracks built to impersonate a real artist or group. The policy extends to Tidal Upload, its independent-artist program, closing an obvious loophole. The company frames the goal simply: royalties should go to people who actually wrote and performed the music. It's a concrete answer to a question streaming services have mostly avoided — not "should AI music exist," but "who gets paid when it does."

related.title: Who Owns AI's Output?
related.hook: You typed the prompt, the AI made the image — so who owns it? The law is genuinely unsettled, and the answer depends on where you are and how much was really you.

related.title: See the Music That Trained AI
related.hook: Ever wonder if your favorite song helped train an AI? The Atlantic dug up four music datasets used to train AI models — two with millions of tracks — and made them searchable by anyone.

flashcards.prompt: What happens to a song Tidal identifies as 100% AI-generated?

choices.text: It gets an AI tag and stops earning royalties or direct-to-fan sales
It's automatically deleted from the platform
Nothing changes — it's treated exactly like human-made music

flashcards.explanation_html: Tidal doesn't ban fully AI-generated tracks outright — it labels them and cuts off their monetization, while still leaving the music up.

flashcards.prompt: Why is Tidal's move described as different from just labeling AI content?
flashcards.back_html: It targets the money directly — no royalties, no direct-to-fan sales — rather than only flagging AI tracks for visibility.
